query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multi-phase eutectic HEAs, the accelerated degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures is driven by the cyclic rupture of protective oxide films at interphase boundaries. This rupture exposes heterogeneous phase interfaces, which then set up local galvanic cells that accelerate both wear and corrosion in a synergistic manner.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, finely segregated eutectic high-entropy alloy displaying coexisting phases (e.g., FCC matrix and σ phase) with intact passivating oxide films along the interphase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Conduct in situ tribocorrosion testing at elevated temperature (~350°C) with integrated electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) under three conditions: combined wear–corrosion, wear-only, and corrosion-only.
generation.conditions: Controlled environment with constant electrolyte composition (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl), identical applied mechanical load for wear, and testing at ~350°C to ensure dynamic oxide film formation and rupture.
generation.structural_mediator: Interphase oxide films present at the boundaries between distinct eutectic phases.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear disrupts the protective oxide film at interphase boundaries, repeatedly exposing the underlying heterogeneous metal surfaces. The compositional differences between the phases (e.g., between FCC and σ) promote localized galvanic couples, thus accelerating corrosion at these sites. The recurrent film rupture and subsequent corrosion weaken the material further, leading to a synergistic increase in both wear and corrosion degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The combined wear–corrosion condition will exhibit a total degradation significantly exceeding the arithmetic sum of isolated wear and corrosion effects. Specifically, both wear volume loss and corrosion current density will be markedly higher than those measured in wear-only or corrosion-only tests.
generation.baseline: Matched tests performed under isolated conditions: one featuring solely mechanical wear (with an inert electrolyte to minimize corrosion) and another featuring only corrosion (in the absence of significant mechanical wear) at the same temperature and electrolyte settings.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in multi-phase eutectic HEAs operating at elevated temperatures (~350°C) under conditions that promote dynamic oxide film formation and rupture; deviations in microstructure or operating temperature may yield different interactions.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of the synergistic effect is uncertain due to limited direct measurements of oxide film dynamics and localized galvanic interactions. Further controlled experiments are needed to refine these metrics.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a set of in situ tribocorrosion experiments on the eutectic HEA under three identical environmental conditions: (1) simultaneous wear and corrosion, (2) wear-only (using an inert electrolyte to suppress corrosion), and (3) corrosion-only (with negligible mechanical wear). Monitor the integrity of the oxide films at interphase boundaries in real time using surface microscopy and EIS.
measurements: Corrosion current density via electrochemical methods
EIS spectra to track oxide film formation/rupture
Surface morphology and interphase boundary analysis through microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the degradation observed under combined wear–corrosion is merely additive (or less) compared to the sum of isolated wear and corrosion conditions, or if in situ monitoring fails to show cyclic rupture of the oxide film at the interphase boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

This study systematically investigates the microstructure evolution, tribological properties, and corrosion mechanisms of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings fabricated via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding under variable laser power conditions. The key findings and implications are summarized as follows: The CoCrFeNiMo coatings exhibited a dual-phase structure comprising FCC and σ phases. At 2250 W, optimized energy density promoted homogeneous dispersion of Fe-Cr-rich σa and Fe-Mo-rich σb phases within the FCC matrix, forming a refined eutectic–hypereutectic hybrid microstructure. The hardness of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coatings increased with laser power, peaking at 738.3 HV0.2 at 2250 W. This improvement was attributed to solution strengthening and second-phase intensification. However, at 2000 W, the hardness decreased due to grain coarsening caused by the extended molten pool duration. At a laser power of 2250 W, the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating exhibited the lowest coefficient of friction (COF = 0.084) and excellent wear resistance. occupying_moves.technique: tribocorrosion testing with in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)
occupying_moves.conditions: Multi-phase eutectic HEA samples tested under three matched conditions – (a) wear only, (b) corrosion only, and (c) combined wear and corrosion at an elevated temperature (e.g., 350°C) with identical mechanical loads and electrolyte chemistry. The tests are designed to isolate the role of surface oxide film removal and interphase boundary degradation.

chosen.technique: tribocorrosion testing combined with in situ EIS and microstructural analysis
chosen.conditions: Conduct experiments on multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy samples under three regimes – isolated wear, isolated corrosion, and their combination at elevated temperature (e.g., 350°C) with controlled mechanical loads and electrolyte environment – to distinguish the contribution of mechanical removal of protective films versus corrosion weakening interphase boundaries.
chosen.why: This approach directly addresses the open question by testing whether the synergistic degradation is due to the continuous removal of a protective oxide film (or weakening of interphase regions) during combined wear-corrosion exposure. By comparing against isolated degradation modes under identical conditions, the proposed mechanism can be clearly falsified if the combined test does not exhibit an accelerated degradation rate beyond the sum of its individual modes. The technique uses standard tribocorrosion methods and in situ EIS, making it a plausible and effective study for a research group specializing in controlled variable experiments in materials science.

frame.system: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy in its as-cast, finely segregated eutectic microstructure, where different phases coexist and potentially interact under service conditions.
frame.goal: To identify and explain a single mechanistic hypothesis that accounts for the accelerated degradation observed under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures, and to quantify how these processes interact relative to a baseline condition.
frame.limitation: Lack of a unified mechanistic understanding that explains why acceleration in degradation occurs under coupled wear–corrosion conditions, especially in multi-phase systems at high temperature.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) established eutectic HEAs as promising due to their finely segregated, dual‐phase microstructures for high-temperature mechanical performance. Later studies (PMC7515071) probed high-temperature wear behavior in similarly complex, multiphase alloys, noting that protective oxide layers could form and influence wear. Subsequent work (PMC12463061) on HEA coatings revealed that under friction, cyclic rupture of oxide films at phase boundaries leads to a mix of adhesive and abrasive wear, with underlying galvanic differences between phases driving corrosion. Taken together, the sequence moved from demonstrating attractive microstructures in eutectic HEAs, to analyzing single-mode degradation, and finally hinting at the interplay between mechanical wear (and its removal of passivating films) and electrochemical effects at phase boundaries. However, prior experiments lacked a controlled baseline to isolate the synergistic impact of concurrent wear and corrosion in multi‐phase structures at elevated temperatures.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved how the dynamic removal and reformation of protective oxide films at the heterogeneous phase interfaces in a multi‐phase eutectic HEA specifically triggers enhanced local galvanic corrosion that, in turn, accelerates overall degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion. In particular, the extent to which interphase boundary damage under high-temperature conditions drives non‐additive (synergistic) acceleration in both wear and corrosion metrics has not been quantified in a controlled experiment.
decision.lever: simultaneous wear–corrosion interaction via in situ tribocorrosion testing with integrated electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)
decision.why: Building on the trend where early studies established the favourable eutectic microstructure and later work suggested that cyclic oxide film rupture at phase interfaces promotes wear and galvanic corrosion, the next logical step is a controlled experiment. By testing three matched conditions (wear only, corrosion only, and combined wear–corrosion) under elevated temperatures (e.g., ~350°C) and identical mechanical and electrolyte conditions, the experiment can isolate the effect of localized oxide film removal at the interphase boundaries. This experiment would provide direct quantitative evidence linking the interplay of mechanical and chemical degradation to accelerated total degradation, thereby testing the hypothesis that interphase boundary disruption is the mechanistic trigger.
